claim: Type I interferons (IFNs) are essential for anti-viral immunity.
source: Type I interferons (IFNs) are essential for anti-viral immunity, but often impair protective immune responses during bacterial infections.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in immunology, supported by citation to Stetson and Medzhitov, 2006 in the Introduction.

claim: Type I interferons often impair protective immune responses during bacterial infections.
source: Type I interferons (IFNs) are essential for anti-viral immunity, but often impair protective immune responses during bacterial infections.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the Introduction and by experimental data showing Ifnar-/- mice have enhanced resistance to bacterial infections.

claim: The Super susceptibility to tuberculosis 1 (Sst1) locus in mice confers resistance to diverse bacterial infections.
source: The Super susceptibility to tuberculosis 1 (Sst1) locus in mice confers resistance to diverse bacterial infections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2005 and Pichugin et al., 2009, and by experimental data showing Sst1S mice are susceptible to multiple bacterial infections.

claim: Sp140 is a gene encoded within the Sst1 locus that represses type I IFN transcription during bacterial infections.
source: Here we provide evidence that Sp140 is a gene encoded within the Sst1 locus that represses type I IFN transcription during bacterial infections.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Sp140-/- mice have elevated type I IFN responses and are susceptible to bacterial infections.

claim: Sp140–/– mice are susceptible to infection by Legionella pneumophila.
source: We generated Sp140–/– mice and found that they are susceptible to infection by Legionella pneumophila and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
evidence: This is directly supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Sp140–/– mice are susceptible to infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: We generated Sp140–/– mice and found that they are susceptible to infection by Legionella pneumophila and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
evidence: This is directly supported by CFU, weight loss, and survival data shown in Figures 2C-F.

claim: Susceptibility of Sp140–/– mice to bacterial infection was rescued by crosses to mice lacking the type I IFN receptor (Ifnar–/–).
source: Susceptibility of Sp140–/– mice to bacterial infection was rescued by crosses to mice lacking the type I IFN receptor (Ifnar–/–).
evidence: This is directly supported by data in Figure 5 showing reduced bacterial burdens and weight loss in Sp140-/- Ifnar-/- mice.

claim: Sp140 is an important negative regulator of type I IFNs that is essential for resistance to bacterial infections.
source: Our results implicate Sp140 as an important negative regulator of type I IFNs that is essential for resistance to bacterial infections.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Sp140-/- mice have elevated type I IFN responses and are susceptible to bacterial infections, which is rescued by Ifnar deletion.

claim: Type I IFNs signal through a cell surface receptor, the interferon alpha and beta receptor (IFNAR), to induce an 'anti-viral state'.
source: Type I IFNs signal through a cell surface receptor, the interferon alpha and beta receptor (IFNAR), to induce an 'anti-viral state' that is characterized by the transcriptional induction of hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) (Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to Schneider et al., 2014.

claim: Many ISGs encode proteins with direct anti-viral activities.
source: Many ISGs encode proteins with direct anti-viral activities.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of interferon biology.

claim: Type I IFNs promote anti-viral responses by cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells.
source: Type I IFNs also promote anti-viral responses by cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology.

claim: Ifnar–/– mice are highly susceptible to most viral infections.
source: Accordingly, Ifnar–/– mice are highly susceptible to most viral infections.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, following from the essential role of type I IFNs in anti-viral immunity.

claim: Many ISGs are also induced by IFN-γ (also called type II IFN).
source: Many ISGs are also induced by IFN-γ (also called type II IFN).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of interferon biology.

claim: Type I and type II IFNs appear to be specialized for the control of different classes of pathogens.
source: However, type I and type II IFNs appear to be specialized for the control of different classes of pathogens (Crisler and Lenz, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crisler and Lenz, 2018.

claim: Type I IFNs are predominantly anti-viral.
source: Whereas type I IFNs are predominantly anti-viral, the ISGs induced by IFN-γ appear to be especially important for the control of diverse intracellular pathogens, including parasites and bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology.

claim: The ISGs induced by IFN-γ appear to be especially important for the control of diverse intracellular pathogens, including parasites and bacteria.
source: Whereas type I IFNs are predominantly anti-viral, the ISGs induced by IFN-γ appear to be especially important for the control of diverse intracellular pathogens, including parasites and bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology.

claim: Type I IFNs play complex roles during bacterial infections.
source: In contrast, type I IFNs play complex roles during bacterial infections (Boxx and Cheng, 2016; Donovan et al., 2017; McNab et al., 2015; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to review articles.

claim: Some ISGs induced by type I IFN, most notably certain guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs), have anti-bacterial activities.
source: Some ISGs induced by type I IFN, most notably certain guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs), have anti-bacterial activities (Pilla-Moffett et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pilla-Moffett et al., 2016.

claim: Other proteins induced by type I IFNs, including interleukin-10 (IL-10) and IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA), impair anti-bacterial immunity.
source: At the same time, other proteins induced by type I IFNs, including interleukin-10 (IL-10) and IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA), impair anti-bacterial immunity (Boxx and Cheng, 2016; Ji et al., 2019; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including the authors' previous work.

claim: The net effect of type I IFN is often to increase susceptibility to bacterial infections.
source: As a result, the net effect of type I IFN is often to increase susceptibility to bacterial infections.
evidence: This is supported by the examples that follow, showing Ifnar-/- mice are more resistant to bacterial infections.

claim: Ifnar–/– mice exhibit enhanced resistance to Listeria monocytogenes.
source: For example, Ifnar–/– mice exhibit enhanced resistance to Listeria monocytogenes (Auerbuch et al., 2004; Carrero et al., 2004; O'Connell et al., 2004) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Donovan et al., 2017; Dorhoi et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2019; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ifnar–/– mice exhibit enhanced resistance to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: For example, Ifnar–/– mice exhibit enhanced resistance to Listeria monocytogenes (Auerbuch et al., 2004; Carrero et al., 2004; O'Connell et al., 2004) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Donovan et al., 2017; Dorhoi et al., 2014; Ji et al., 2019; Mayer-Barber et al., 2014; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including the authors' previous work.

claim: Multiple mechanisms appear to explain resistance of Ifnar–/– mice to L. monocytogenes, including a negative effect of type I IFNs on protective IFN-γ signaling.
source: Multiple mechanisms appear to explain resistance of Ifnar–/– mice to L. monocytogenes, including a negative effect of type I IFNs on protective IFN-γ signaling (Rayamajhi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rayamajhi et al., 2010.

claim: Diverse mechanisms underlie the negative effects of type I IFNs during M. tuberculosis infection, including alterations of eicosanoid production and the induction of IL-1Ra.
source: Likewise, diverse mechanisms underlie the negative effects of type I IFNs during M. tuberculosis infection, including alterations of eicosanoid production (Mayer-Barber et al., 2014) and the induction of IL-1Ra (Ji et al., 2019), both of which impair protective IL-1 responses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mayer-Barber et al., 2014 and Ji et al., 2019.

claim: Alterations of eicosanoid production and the induction of IL-1Ra both impair protective IL-1 responses.
source: Likewise, diverse mechanisms underlie the negative effects of type I IFNs during M. tuberculosis infection, including alterations of eicosanoid production (Mayer-Barber et al., 2014) and the induction of IL-1Ra (Ji et al., 2019), both of which impair protective IL-1 responses.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mayer-Barber et al., 2014 and Ji et al., 2019.

claim: The Sst1 locus encompasses about 10M base pairs of mouse chromosome 1, a region that contains approximately 50 genes.
source: The Sst1 locus encompasses about 10M base pairs of mouse chromosome 1, a region that contains approximately 50 genes.
evidence: This is a factual description of the genetic locus, likely based on genome annotation.

claim: Mice harboring the susceptible (S) haplotype of Sst1, derived from the C3H/HeBFeJ mouse strain, succumb relatively rapidly to M. tuberculosis infection as compared to isogenic mice harboring the resistant (R) Sst1 haplotype (derived from C57BL/6 mice).
source: Mice harboring the susceptible (S) haplotype of Sst1, derived from the C3H/HeBFeJ mouse strain, succumb relatively rapidly to M. tuberculosis infection as compared to isogenic mice harboring the resistant (R) Sst1 haplotype (derived from C57BL/6 mice).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Sst1 locus, supported by the survival data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Sst1S mice exhibit enhanced susceptibility to L. monocytogenes.
source: Likewise, Sst1S mice also exhibit enhanced susceptibility to L. monocytogenes (Boyartchuk et al., 2004; Pan et al., 2005) and Chlamydia pneumoniae (He et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyartchuk et al., 2004 and Pan et al., 2005.

claim: Sst1S mice exhibit enhanced susceptibility to Chlamydia pneumoniae.
source: Likewise, Sst1S mice also exhibit enhanced susceptibility to L. monocytogenes (Boyartchuk et al., 2004; Pan et al., 2005) and Chlamydia pneumoniae (He et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2013.

claim: The susceptibility of Sst1S mice to M. tuberculosis was reversed by crossing to Ifnar–/– mice.
source: The susceptibility of Sst1S mice to M. tuberculosis was reversed by crossing to Ifnar–/– mice (Ji et al., 2019), thereby demonstrating the causative role of type I IFNs in driving the susceptibility phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Ji et al., 2019) and by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Type I IFNs play a causative role in driving the susceptibility phenotype of Sst1S mice.
source: The susceptibility of Sst1S mice to M. tuberculosis was reversed by crossing to Ifnar–/– mice (Ji et al., 2019), thereby demonstrating the causative role of type I IFNs in driving the susceptibility phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue of susceptibility in Sst1S Ifnar-/- mice.

claim: Heterozygous deficiency of Il1rn (encoding IL-1 receptor antagonist) was sufficient to almost entirely reverse the susceptibility of Sst1S mice to M. tuberculosis.
source: Although multiple type I IFN-induced genes are likely responsible for the detrimental effects of type I IFNs during bacterial infections, heterozygous deficiency of a single type I IFN-induced gene, Il1rn (encoding IL-1 receptor antagonist), was sufficient to almost entirely reverse the susceptibility of Sst1S mice to M. tuberculosis (Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Ji et al., 2019).

claim: The Sst1R haplotype is dominant over the Sst1S haplotype.
source: The Sst1R haplotype is dominant over the Sst1S haplotype, suggesting that Sst1R encodes a protective factor that is absent from Sst1S mice (Pan et al., 2005; Pichugin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2005 and Pichugin et al., 2009.

claim: Sst1R encodes a protective factor that is absent from Sst1S mice.
source: The Sst1R haplotype is dominant over the Sst1S haplotype, suggesting that Sst1R encodes a protective factor that is absent from Sst1S mice (Pan et al., 2005; Pichugin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the dominance of the Sst1R haplotype.

claim: Sp110 (also known as Ipr1) is an Sst1-encoded gene that is transcribed selectively in Sst1R mice.
source: By comparing gene expression in Sst1R versus Sst1S mice, Sp110 (also known as Ipr1) was discovered as an Sst1-encoded gene that is transcribed selectively in Sst1R mice (Pan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2005.

claim: Transgenic expression of Sp110 in Sst1S mice partially restored resistance to M. tuberculosis and L. monocytogenes.
source: Transgenic expression of Sp110 in Sst1S mice partially restored resistance to M. tuberculosis and L. monocytogenes (Pan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2005.

claim: The causative role of Sp110 in conferring resistance to bacterial infections was not confirmed by the generation of Sp110-deficient B6 mice.
source: However, the causative role of Sp110 in conferring resistance to bacterial infections was not confirmed by the generation of Sp110-deficient B6 mice.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 1 showing Sp110-/- mice are resistant to M. tuberculosis.

claim: Null mutations of human SP110 are associated with VODI (hepatic veno-occlusive disease with immunodeficiency syndrome, OMIM 235550), but not mycobacterial diseases.
source: Null mutations of human SP110 are associated with VODI (hepatic veno-occlusive disease with immunodeficiency syndrome, OMIM 235550), but not mycobacterial diseases (Roscioli et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roscioli et al., 2006.

claim: Some studies have found polymorphisms in SP110 to be associated with susceptibility to TB, though not consistently so across different ethnic groups.
source: Some studies have found polymorphisms in SP110 to be associated with susceptibility to TB, though not consistently so across different ethnic groups (Chang et al., 2018; Fox et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2012; Png et al., 2012; Thye et al., 2006; Tosh et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genetic association studies.

claim: In humans and mice, SP110 is a part of the speckled protein (SP) family of nuclear proteins, consisting of SP100, SP110, and SP140 (and SP140L in humans only).
source: In humans and mice, SP110 is a part of the speckled protein (SP) family of nuclear proteins, consisting of SP100, SP110, and SP140 (and SP140L in humans only) (Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SP protein family, supported by citation to Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020.

claim: The SP family members exhibit a high degree of similarity to AIRE, a transcriptional regulator that promotes tolerance to self-antigens by inducing their expression in thymic epithelial cells.
source: The SP family members also exhibit a high degree of similarity to AIRE, a transcriptional regulator that promotes tolerance to self-antigens by inducing their expression in thymic epithelial cells (Anderson and Su, 2016; Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020; Perniola and Musco, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AIRE and its relationship to SP proteins, supported by multiple citations.

claim: All members of the SP-AIRE family in both mice and humans have an N-terminal SP100 domain that appears to function as a homotypic protein-protein interaction domain.
source: All members of the SP-AIRE family in both mice and humans have an N-terminal SP100 domain that appears to function as a homotypic protein-protein interaction domain (Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020; Huoh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020 and Huoh et al., 2020.

claim: The SP100 domain is closely related to the caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD), though SP family members are not believed to activate caspases.
source: The SP100 domain is closely related to the caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD), though SP family members are not believed to activate caspases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structural relationship between SP100 and CARD domains.

claim: SP-AIRE proteins contain a DNA-binding SAND domain.
source: SP-AIRE proteins also contain a DNA-binding SAND domain (Bottomley et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bottomley et al., 2001.

claim: Certain SP isoforms, including all human full-length SP family members and mouse SP140, include a plant homeobox domain (PHD) and a bromodomain (BRD).
source: Certain SP isoforms, including all human full-length SP family members and mouse SP140, also include a plant homeobox domain (PHD) and a bromodomain (BRD) (Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fraschilla and Jeffrey, 2020.

claim: The genes encoding SP family proteins are linked in a small cluster in both mouse and human genomes and are inducible by IFN-γ in a variety of cell lines.
source: The genes encoding SP family proteins are linked in a small cluster in both mouse and human genomes and are inducible by IFN-γ in a variety of cell lines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genomic organization and regulation of SP genes.

claim: The mouse Sp100/110/140 gene cluster is adjacent to a highly repetitive 'homogenously staining region' (HSR) of chromosome 1 that remains poorly assembled in the most recent genome assembly due to the presence of as many as 40 near-identical repeats of Sp110-like sequences.
source: The mouse Sp100/110/140 gene cluster is adjacent to a highly repetitive 'homogenously staining region' (HSR) of chromosome 1 that remains poorly assembled in the most recent genome assembly due to the presence of as many as 40 near-identical repeats of Sp110-like sequences (Pan et al., 2005; Weichenhan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2005 and Weichenhan et al., 2001.

claim: Most of the repeated Sp110-like sequences in the HSR appear to be either incomplete copies of Sp110 or pseudogenes that are not believed to be translated.
source: Most of these repeated Sp110-like sequences in the HSR appear to be either incomplete copies of Sp110 or pseudogenes that are not believed to be translated, but their presence has nevertheless complicated genetic targeting and analysis of the SP gene family.
evidence: This is inferred from genome annotation and the difficulty in genetic targeting.

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMMs) from B6.Sst1S mice lack expression of Sp110 protein.
source: We first confirmed that bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMMs) from B6.Sst1S mice lack expression of Sp110 protein (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1A.

claim: Three independent Sp110–/– lines (lines 61, 65, and 71) were generated using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: We generated three independent Sp110–/– lines, denoted as lines 61, 65, and 71 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is documented in the text and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All three Sp110–/– lines lacked expression of Sp110, as verified using three different antibodies.
source: All three lines lacked expression of Sp110, as verified using three different antibodies (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly shown by immunoblot data in Figure 1A using three different antibodies.

claim: Sp110–/– mice are viable and are born at normal Mendelian ratios and litter sizes.
source: Sp110–/– mice are viable and are born at normal Mendelian ratios and litter sizes.
evidence: This is an observation from breeding the mice.

claim: At day 25 post-infection with M. tuberculosis, Sp110–/– lungs resembled those of wild-type B6 mice.
source: At day 25 post-infection, Sp110–/– lungs resembled those of wild-type B6 mice (Figure 1B) and harbored fewer bacteria than the lungs of B6.Sst1S mice, similar to both the B6 and Sp110+/– littermates (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by histology in Figure 1B.

claim: At day 25 post-infection with M. tuberculosis, Sp110–/– lungs harbored fewer bacteria than the lungs of B6.Sst1S mice, similar to both the B6 and Sp110+/– littermates.
source: At day 25 post-infection, Sp110–/– lungs resembled those of wild-type B6 mice (Figure 1B) and harbored fewer bacteria than the lungs of B6.Sst1S mice, similar to both the B6 and Sp110+/– littermates (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown by CFU data in Figure 1C.

claim: The survival of infected Sp110–/– mice was indistinguishable from B6 mice, and mice of both genotypes survived considerably longer than the B6.Sst1S mice.
source: Likewise, the survival of infected Sp110–/– mice was indistinguishable from B6 mice, and mice of both genotypes survived considerably longer than the B6.Sst1S mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown by survival data in Figure 1D.

claim: The loss of Sp110 is not sufficient to replicate the susceptibility to M. tuberculosis associated with the Sst1S locus.
source: Thus, despite the absence of Sp110 from Sst1S mice, our results indicate that the loss of Sp110 is not sufficient to replicate the susceptibility to M. tuberculosis associated with the Sst1S locus.
evidence: This is concluded from the resistance of Sp110-/- mice to M. tuberculosis shown in Figures 1B-D.

claim: IFN-γ treated BMMs from B6.Sst1S mice do not produce SP140 protein.
source: Immunoblot confirmed that IFN-γ treated BMMs from B6.Sst1S mice do not produce SP140 protein (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Two independent lines of Sp140–/– mice were generated on a pure B6 background using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: We therefore used CRISPR/Cas9 to generate two independent lines of Sp140–/– mice on a pure B6 background (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is documented in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Sp140–/– line 1 lacks expression of SP140 protein.
source: Our analysis focused primarily on line 1, which we found lacked expression of SP140 protein (Figure 2B) but retains the production of SP110 protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Sp140–/– line 1 retains the production of SP110 protein.
source: Our analysis focused primarily on line 1, which we found lacked expression of SP140 protein (Figure 2B) but retains the production of SP110 protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Sp140–/– mice are viable, fertile, and born at the expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Like Sp110–/– and Sst1S mice, Sp140–/– mice are viable, fertile, and born at the expected Mendelian ratios.
evidence: This is an observation from breeding the mice.

claim: When infected with M. tuberculosis, Sp140–/– mice exhibited high bacterial burdens in their lungs, similar to B6.Sst1S mice and significantly greater than B6, Sp110–/– or Sp140+/– littermate mice at day 28 post-infection.
source: When infected with M. tuberculosis, however, Sp140–/– mice exhibited high bacterial burdens in their lungs, similar to B6.Sst1S mice and significantly greater than B6, Sp110–/– or Sp140+/– littermate mice at day 28 post-infection (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by CFU data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Sp140–/– and B6.Sst1S lungs showed moderately increased granulocyte infiltration by 25 days post M. tuberculosis infection.
source: We found that Sp140–/– and B6.Sst1S lungs showed moderately increased granulocyte infiltration by 25 days post infection, with apparently more severe infiltration in Sp140–/– mice than in B6.Sst1S mice, though this difference is not statistically significant.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some areas of necrosis were discernible in the Sp140–/– lungs at 25 days post M. tuberculosis infection.
source: We could also discern some areas of necrosis in the Sp140–/– lungs, although our samples were taken at an early timepoint that precedes the formation of hypoxic lesions observed in B6.Sst1S lungs upon M. tuberculosis infection (Harper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increased susceptibility of Sp140–/– mice to M. tuberculosis was accompanied by significant weight loss and shortened survival.
source: The increased susceptibility of Sp140–/– mice was accompanied by significant weight loss and shortened survival upon infection with M. tuberculosis, again phenocopying the B6.Sst1S mice (Figure 2E-F).
evidence: This is shown by weight and survival data in Figures 2E-F.

claim: Both independent lines of Sp140–/– mice were similarly susceptible to M. tuberculosis.
source: Both of the independent lines of Sp140–/– mice were similarly susceptible to M. tuberculosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown by CFU data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both B6.Sst1S and Sp140–/– mice were more susceptible to the intracellular Gram-negative bacterium L. pneumophila, as compared to the B6 and Sp110–/– mice.
source: We also found that both B6.Sst1S and Sp140–/– mice were more susceptible to the intracellular Gram-negative bacterium L. pneumophila, as compared to the B6 and Sp110–/– mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is shown by CFU data in Figure 2G.

claim: The guide RNA used to disrupt exon 3 of Sp140 may have also disrupted uncharacterized Sp140-like genes.
source: It is possible that the guide RNA we used to disrupt exon 3 of Sp140 also disrupted these uncharacterized Sp140-like genes, though it is not clear if these uncharacterized Sp140-like genes give rise to functional proteins.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of Sp140-like sequences in the genome.

claim: Several edited Sp140-like exons were found in Sp140–/– mice by deep sequencing of amplicons.
source: Although we found evidence for several edited Sp140-like exons in our Sp140–/– mice, only one of these edited off-target genes was found to be detectably expressed from analysis of RNA-seq data from M. tuberculosis-infected lungs, and this off-target appeared to be edited in only one of our founder lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown by amplicon sequencing data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only one edited off-target Sp140-like gene was detectably expressed in M. tuberculosis-infected lungs, and this off-target was edited in only one founder line.
source: Although we found evidence for several edited Sp140-like exons in our Sp140–/– mice, only one of these edited off-target genes was found to be detectably expressed from analysis of RNA-seq data from M. tuberculosis-infected lungs, and this off-target appeared to be edited in only one of our founder lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown by amplicon sequencing and RNA-seq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Mutation of Sp140 itself is the most parsimonious explanation for susceptibility of Sp140–/– mice.
source: Thus, mutation of Sp140 itself is the most parsimonious explanation for susceptibility of our Sp140–/– mice, a conclusion further supported by complementation of the mutation in BMMs (see below, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the off-target analysis and complementation experiments.

claim: The lack of expression of Sp140 in B6.Sst1S mice explains the broad susceptibility of these mice to bacterial infections.
source: Collectively our results strongly suggest that the lack of expression of Sp140 in B6.Sst1S mice explains the broad susceptibility of these mice to bacterial infections.
evidence: This is concluded from the phenotypic similarity between Sp140-/- and B6.Sst1S mice.

claim: TNFα induces higher levels of type I IFN-induced genes in Sst1S BMMs as compared to B6 BMMs.
source: We and others previously reported that TNFα induces higher levels of type I IFN-induced genes in Sst1S BMMs as compared to B6 BMMs (Bhattacharya et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bhattacharya et al., 2021 and the authors' previous work (Ji et al., 2019).

claim: Higher levels of Ifnb transcripts were observed in the lungs of B6.Sst1S mice infected with M. tuberculosis, as compared to infected B6 mice.
source: We also observed higher levels of Ifnb transcripts in the lungs of B6.Sst1S mice infected with M. tuberculosis, as compared to infected B6 mice (Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Ji et al., 2019).

claim: Sp140–/– BMMs exhibited elevated expression of Ifnb and ISGs when stimulated with TNFα.
source: Similar to B6.Sst1S BMMs, Sp140–/– BMMs also exhibited elevated expression of Ifnb and ISGs when stimulated with TNFα (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is shown by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The enhanced IFN phenotype of Sp140–/– BMMs was complemented by transducing Sp140–/– BMMs with a retrovirus expressing an Sp140 cDNA.
source: Importantly, we were also able to complement the enhanced IFN phenotype of Sp140–/– BMMs by transducing Sp140–/– BMMs with a retrovirus expressing an Sp140 cDNA driven by a minimal CMV promoter (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Repression of Ifnb by overexpression of Sp140 in Sp140–/– BMMs was selective, as Sp140 overexpression did not repress the transcription of Tnfa induced by TNFα.
source: Repression of Ifnb by overexpression of Sp140 in Sp140–/– BMMs was selective, as Sp140 overexpression did not repress the transcription of Tnfa induced by TNFα (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Both B6.Sst1S and Sp140–/– BMMs show increased cell death in vitro upon stimulation with polyI:C compared to B6 BMMs, as measured by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release.
source: In addition to enhanced type I IFN responses to TNFα, we also observed that both B6.Sst1S and Sp140–/– BMMs show increased cell death in vitro upon stimulation with polyI:C compared to B6 BMMs, as measured by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by LDH release data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enhanced polyI:C-induced LDH release in both Sp140–/– and B6.Sst1S BMMs was blunted upon genetic deletion of Ifnar.
source: The enhanced polyI:C-induced LDH release in both Sp140–/– and B6.Sst1S BMMs was blunted upon genetic deletion of Ifnar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with type I IFNs playing an important role in the cell death phenotype.
evidence: This is shown by LDH release data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Type I IFNs play an important role in the polyI:C-induced cell death phenotype of Sp140–/– and B6.Sst1S BMMs.
source: The enhanced polyI:C-induced LDH release in both Sp140–/– and B6.Sst1S BMMs was blunted upon genetic deletion of Ifnar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with type I IFNs playing an important role in the cell death phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of cell death by Ifnar deletion.

claim: When infected with M. tuberculosis, the lungs of Sp140–/– and B6.Sst1S mice exhibited higher levels of Ifnb transcript as compared to B6, Sp110–/–, and Sp140+/– littermate mice.

claim: Loss of Ifnar reduced bacterial burdens in Sp140–/– mice at day 25 post M. tuberculosis infection, similar to those seen in B6 mice.

claim: Type I IFN signaling is responsible for the susceptibility of Sp140–/– mice to M. tuberculosis.

claim: Type I IFN signaling is partially responsible for the susceptibility of Sp140–/– mice to L. pneumophila.

claim: Type I IFN-driven immunity is generally critical for defense against viruses.
source: For example, type I IFN-driven immunity is generally critical for defense against viruses (Schneider et al., 2014; Stetson and Medzhitov, 2006), whereas type II IFN (IFN-γ)-driven immunity mediates resistance to intracellular pathogens (Crisler and Lenz, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Type II IFN (IFN-γ)-driven immunity mediates resistance to intracellular pathogens.
source: For example, type I IFN-driven immunity is generally critical for defense against viruses (Schneider et al., 2014; Stetson and Medzhitov, 2006), whereas type II IFN (IFN-γ)-driven immunity mediates resistance to intracellular pathogens (Crisler and Lenz, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: IL-1 is important for inducing neutrophil and other responses against extracellular pathogens.
source: Additionally, IL-1 is important for inducing neutrophil and other responses against extracellular pathogens (Mantovani et al., 2019), and IL-4/–13 (type 2 immunity) orchestrates responses to helminths and other parasites (Locksley, 1994).

claim: IL-4/–13 (type 2 immunity) orchestrates responses to helminths and other parasites.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Negative feedback is essential to enforce choices between possible types of immune responses.

claim: Negative regulation of IFN-γ/IL-1 by type I IFN is likely beneficial to limit immunopathology during viral infections.
source: Although negative regulation of IFN-γ/IL-1 by type I IFN is likely beneficial to limit immunopathology during viral infections, Sst1S mice provide an example of how excessive or inappropriate negative regulation by type I IFN can also be detrimental during bacterial infections (He et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the general principle of limiting immunopathology.

claim: Sst1S mice provide an example of how excessive or inappropriate negative regulation by type I IFN can be detrimental during bacterial infections.
source: Although negative regulation of IFN-γ/IL-1 by type I IFN is likely beneficial to limit immunopathology during viral infections, Sst1S mice provide an example of how excessive or inappropriate negative regulation by type I IFN can also be detrimental during bacterial infections (He et al., 2013; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and by the data showing Sst1S mice are susceptible to bacterial infections due to type I IFN.

claim: The Sst1 locus was first described in 2005.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2005.

claim: Further genetic analysis of the Sst1 locus has been hindered by its extreme repetitiveness and the concomitant difficulty in generating specific loss-of-function mutations in Sst1-linked genes.
